screens.body:
A file system is how the OS organizes raw bytes on a disk into named files and folders you can actually use. Without it, a disk is just a giant pile of bits.

NTFS (Windows), APFS (Mac), ext4 (Linux) — different file systems, same job: names, organization, and rules.

options: Organizes disk bytes into named files and folders
Is a type of database server
check.question: A file system…

screens.heading: What is a file system?
screens.keyPoint: File systems turn disk bits into named files.

screens.body:
A file holds data. A directory (folder) holds names of files and other directories — it's really just a special file containing a list.

On Linux, almost everything is a file: your disk, your keyboard, even a process's info. One simple idea, applied everywhere.

options: A special file listing other files and directories
check.question: A directory is…

screens.heading: Files and directories
screens.keyPoint: Directories are lists of names — special files themselves.

screens.body:
A path says where a file lives. Absolute paths start from the root: /home/ama/notes.txt. Relative paths start from where you are now: notes.txt or ../photos.

Relative paths break when "where you are" changes — the classic cause of "file not found" bugs in deployed apps.
screens.heading: Paths: absolute vs relative
screens.keyPoint: Relative paths depend on where you stand.

screens.body:
Every file has permissions: who can read (r), write (w), and execute (x) it. Unix splits "who" into three: owner, group, and everyone else.

rwxr-xr-x means: owner can do everything, group and others can read and execute but not write. Your private keys should never be readable by "everyone else".

options: Read and execute, but not write
check.question: In rwxr-xr-x, 'others' can…

screens.heading: Permissions: who can do what
screens.keyPoint: rwx for owner, group, and others.

screens.body:
Every file carries metadata: size, owner, creation and modification times, permissions. On Unix, most of it lives in an inode — a data structure for the file.

Fun detail: the file's NAME isn't in the inode. Names live in the directory listing. That's why one file can have multiple names (hard links).

options: The directory listing, not the file itself
check.question: A file's name lives in…

screens.heading: Metadata: data about data
screens.keyPoint: The name lives in the directory, not the file.

screens.body:
If power dies mid-write, a file system could be left half-updated and corrupted. Journaling prevents that: the FS writes its intentions to a journal (diary) first.

After a crash, it replays the journal to finish or undo interrupted work. That's why modern systems usually reboot cleanly instead of losing your files.

options: Logs intended changes so crashes don't corrupt data
check.question: Journaling…

screens.heading: Journaling: surviving crashes
screens.keyPoint: A diary of intentions protects against crashes.

screens.body:
"Permission denied" on your deploy? That's file permissions. Your .env with API keys? That file should be readable only by you (chmod 600).

And every "file not found" after deploying to Vercel is usually a path problem: code that assumed it was running in a folder it isn't. Absolute vs relative — it matters.
screens.heading: Why this matters for you
screens.keyPoint: Permissions and paths explain most deploy file errors.
